progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From b08: gene pool, allele frequency, genetic drift, bottleneck and founder effect, gene flow. From bio-m5-b01: the Cavendish banana is a clone threatened by TR4; asexual copying gives offspring with the same alleles. From b09: copying keeps a combination of alleles together; biotechnology inserts genes (recombinant DNA). From b10: Bt cotton cuts insecticide spraying; a field of one crop holds little biodiversity. From b11: judging plausibility and "could, if". From Year 11 (Module 4, ecosystem dynamics): species, communities, habitats and ecosystems. Not assumed: the three levels of biodiversity as named levels, baseline, herbicide-tolerant crops, QCAV-4, the northern white rhino programme.
progression.startsWith: Choose a crop or conservation case and a comparison baseline. The video opens: Two rescues.
progression.stopsAfter: defining biodiversity at three levels (genetic: alleles in a population or species; species: species in an area; ecosystem: habitats and communities across a region) and tracing each separately; explaining that an effect is a change from a stated baseline, and that the same field can be a gain on one baseline and a loss on another; tracing the resistant Cavendish (a gene from a wild banana protects survival, but the crop stays one clone, so its gene pool stays narrow); tracing crop fields at the species and ecosystem levels (fewer sprays can leave more insect species than sprayed fields; whole-field herbicide removes weeds and wildflowers insects use; land sparing only if land is protected); describing the northern white rhino programme (eggs from one female, banked sperm, southern white surrogates) and tracing it (it could preserve the subspecies and some of its genetic diversity, but adds a species to an area only if white rhinos are absent from that baseline area; genetic bottleneck; a stem-cell route that could widen the gene pool; ecosystem role decades away); explaining that yield is not a level of biodiversity and writing a level-by-level conclusion; applying this to an unseen gene-flow item and an unseen restoration claim.
progression.nextLesson: how to weigh benefits against biodiversity risks and reach a justified, conditional judgement (route entry bio-m6-b13).

teaching.task: A resistant banana and a rhino rescue both use genetic techniques to stop something dying out. But does each one increase biodiversity, and how do you trace the effect?
teaching.causalExplanation: Causes: why one answer is not enough (a technique can move levels in different directions, 2); why the same field gives opposite answers (the baseline changes, 3); why Cavendish is vulnerable and stays narrow after modification (suckers copy one genotype; one added resistance trait does not add variety, 4); why Bt cotton can raise insect species and herbicide tolerance can lower them (fewer sprays against whole-field weed removal, 5); why land sparing is conditional (yield does not protect land by itself, 5); why saving a subspecies is not a species gain unless white rhinos are absent from the baseline area (7); why the rhino rescue starts a bottleneck (one female's eggs, few males, 7); why the stem-cell route could widen it (more founders, 7); why yield is not biodiversity (it measures production, 8). Visible case: one board, two columns, arrows with baseline chips. Video advantage: the amber gene sliding into one repeated strip, insects leaving a sprayed crop row, the gene-pool cluster squeezing through a bottleneck and regaining colours. Thinking opportunities: two unseen items. Reading load: at most about three bright text items; the attempt 2 card is the densest frame and is the task.
teaching.conversationalApproach: A disease-resistant Cavendish banana and the northern white rhino rescue both use genetic techniques to stop something dying out, so the question is whether each increases biodiversity and how to trace the effect; biodiversity is split into genetic, species and ecosystem levels, each effect is a change from a named baseline, the resistant banana adds one resistance trait but the crop stays one clone, crop fields can gain or lose insect species depending on the trait and baseline, and the rhino rescue could preserve the subspecies and some of its genetic diversity, adding a species to an area only if white rhinos are absent from that baseline area, while starting a genetic bottleneck that a stem-cell route could widen; yield is not a level, so answers trace each level on a stated baseline. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: Two rescues. Every Cavendish banana plant is a clone, and the fungus TR4 can kill any of them, so Australian scientists added a resistance gene from a wild banana. And the northern white rhino is down to two females, so scientists are making rhino embryos in the lab. Both use genetic techniques to stop something dying out. But does each one actually increase biodiversity? That depends on which level you look at, and what you compare it with.
teaching.understandingCheck: 10a is an explain item: a herbicide-tolerant crop beside a small wild relative population that can cross with it, with herbicide sprayed at the field edge; explain how this could reduce the wild population's genetic diversity. It applies b08's gene flow and Year 11 selection to scene 2's genetic level. 10c is an evaluate item: the claim that planting blight-resistant modified chestnuts crossed with wild survivors will improve biodiversity. It tests the full route stop (trace each level, name the baseline, judge). Each ends "Pause here to answer." with a 10 s countdown; the full card stays on screen during and after the countdown. Each feedback is brief (about 25 to 30 s): answer, key reason, the givens underlined in the question strip as they are used, one crossed-out classic mistake. No givens card.
teaching.curriculumScope: B6-IQ2-01: "investigate the uses and applications of biotechnology (past, present and future), including: (ACSBL087)", with the listed sub-point this video carries: "evaluating the changes to the Earth's biodiversity due to genetic techniques". B6-IQ3-06: "evaluate the effect on biodiversity of using biotechnology in agriculture". The other B6-IQ2-01 sub-points belong to b10 and b11. Both dotpoints are shared with b13: this video owns the tracing half (name the level, name the baseline, say which way each level moves and why), and b13 owns the weighing half (benefits against biodiversity risks, a justified conditional judgement across cases). Update the ledger rows when this design passes review. The verbs: "evaluate" is carried by attempt 2 (evaluate a claim level by level, ending in a judgement; what-markers-reward: "test the thing named in the question against the evidence and reach a supported judgement"); attempt 1 uses "explain" on the site's own analyse pathway (gene flow into a wild relative). The HSC marker-reported fault "generic claims about biotechnology without explaining its actual effect on biodiversity" (`../research/question-types-bio-m6.md`, 2019 Q24) is the fault scene 8 and both feedbacks target.

design.visualSystem: One levels board throughout: three horizontal rows, top to bottom "ecosystem", "species", "genetic", each with a small coded zoom icon at its left (a landscape of three habitat patches; four different species outlines; a slim allele strip with coloured rings, b01's `AlleleRing` style). Case columns sit to the right of the row labels; each column has a baseline chip at its top ("compared with ...") and a mark cell in each row: an up arrow (more diversity), a down arrow (less), a level dash (no change) or a grey "?" (uncertain), never a score. The crop column (scenes 4 and 5) uses `b1-banana-plantation-tr4-v1.png`, the new `m6-banana-wild-vs-cavendish-v1.png`, `b1-varied-seedlings-v1.png`, `m6-bt-cotton-v1.png` and `m6-field-monoculture-mixed-v1.png`. The conservation column (scenes 6 and 7) uses `m6-northern-white-rhino-v1.png` (once for Najin and Fatu, once small and tinted for the southern white surrogate, always labelled in code), `m6-icsi-v1.png`, `m6-insemination-straw-tank-v1.png` (the dewar, labelled "frozen cells and sperm") and coded gene-pool rings. Clutter rule (owner, 19 Oct): at most about three bright text items at once besides the small grey row labels; each tag fades when the next cue lands; the column not being discussed dims to grey.
